justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users, with wide carriageways, planted medians, and visible sidewalks on both sides rather than forcing all movement into a narrow corridor.
Accessibility is moderate because the sidewalks appear broad and relatively flat, but no clearly visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings can be confirmed from this view.
Fairness is supported by the presence of a bus stop on the left side, indicating that non-drivers have some access to the corridor, not only private car users.
Equity is limited by the dominant amount of asphalt devoted to motor traffic compared with the less prominent pedestrian and cycling space visible at the street edge.
safety: Traffic safety appears relatively strong because the road is wide, sightlines are long, and lane markings are clear, giving drivers ample visibility and reaction distance.
Streetlights are installed continuously along both sides of the road, which likely improves nighttime visibility and perceived security.
The planted median and edge landscaping help organize space and reduce the feeling of uncontrolled mixing between directions of travel.
Safety is weakened for crossing pedestrians and cyclists because no nearby zebra crossing, signalized crossing, or clearly protected bicycle facility is visible in the foreground.
livability: The corridor feels orderly and calm, with generous greenery, trimmed hedges, and mature trees contributing to a pleasant everyday environment.
A bus stop and adjacent large buildings suggest this street serves daily functions and connects to surrounding residential or institutional destinations.
Livability is somewhat reduced by the low level of visible street activity; there are very few people, storefronts, or active ground-floor uses evident along the road.
The very wide roadway gives the space a vehicular scale, which can make the corridor feel less socially vibrant despite its clean and maintained appearance.
sustainability: The bus stop visible on the left supports public transport use, which is a positive low-carbon mobility feature.
Continuous trees, lawn strips, hedges, and planted medians provide urban green infrastructure and help with cooling, air quality, and stormwater absorption.
The street appears well maintained and spacious, but the large paved road surface implies a high land allocation to private motor traffic, which reduces overall sustainability performance.
No clearly marked protected cycle lane or visible bicycle parking is present, limiting support for active, low-emission transport.
aesthetics: The streetscape has strong visual order, with aligned streetlights, consistent building setbacks, and a symmetrical boulevard composition.
Trees, hedges, and landscaped verges soften the corridor and enhance visual quality against the large road surface.
The pavement, curbs, and planting appear clean and well maintained, contributing to a polished and high-quality appearance.
Tall residential buildings on the right and the modern low-rise building on the left create a coherent contemporary urban image with clear skyline definition.
comfort: Thermal comfort is fairly good because both sides of the street include rows of trees and landscaped strips that can provide some shade, especially near the sidewalks.
Physical comfort appears adequate since the sidewalks look wide, smooth, and separated from traffic by planting buffers.
Psychological comfort benefits from the low traffic volume visible in the scene, the uncluttered layout, and long open sightlines.
Comfort is reduced somewhat by the broad expanse of asphalt and limited visible street furniture such as benches or sheltered resting places.
walkability: Walkability is supported by the presence of continuous sidewalks on both sides and by landscaped buffers separating pedestrians from moving vehicles.
The sidewalk environment appears wide and unobstructed, which is favorable for routine walking and side-by-side movement.
Walkability is limited because no nearby marked crosswalk or pedestrian-priority crossing treatment is visible, making road crossing potentially difficult on such a wide boulevard.
The street edge lacks obvious active frontages or frequent entrances at eye level, so walking may feel less engaging despite the clean and green setting.
bikeability: Bikeability is only moderate to low because no clearly marked or protected bike lane is visible along the roadway.
The width of the road and relatively orderly traffic environment may allow experienced cyclists to ride, but comfort for most users is reduced without dedicated cycling space.
The landscaped edges and median help organize the corridor, yet they do not substitute for physical bicycle protection or clear cycle markings.
No bicycle parking, bike signals, or intersection cycling treatments are visible, which weakens convenience and network legibility for cyclists.
